subtype: Approach: cutting losses on a low-yield channel [Revision]
passage: I'm Sumit. Thirty applications through a single job site, six weeks, zero replies. Not even a rejection. I kept telling myself the thirty-first would be the one, because stopping felt like failing. Then I looked at my hours: about ten a week, going into a channel that never answered. So I stopped. Same ten hours, moved: five to alumni messages, three to the college placement cell, two to polishing my resume. Zubin, an alumnus at a mid-sized company, replied within two days and offered to refer me for a junior role. The placement cell also passed my resume to two recruiters. It's early. But for the first time, things are replying.

qa.q: How many applications had Sumit sent on the portal?
qa.a: Sumit had sent thirty applications through a single job site.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling before stopping?
qa.a: Sumit was stubborn and worried, since stopping felt like failing.

qa.q: What could Sumit measure to know when to cut a channel?
qa.a: Sumit could track replies per hour spent, and shift time when a fair trial brings none.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Sumit's message?
qa.a: Zubin seems willing to help, since Zubin replied within two days and offered a referral.

grounding: After thirty applications on one portal with no replies, the student drops it and shifts the same time to alumni referrals and the placement cell.

subtype: Approach: cutting losses on a low-yield channel [Revision]
passage:
Placement cell note, Tuesday. Student: Rajni, final-year B.Com.
Rajni came in today with a printout of her portal history: thirty applications in five weeks on one large job site, zero replies. She said, "I keep thinking the next one will work." We looked at it together. Same kind of role each time, a crowded site, and nobody on the other end who knows her. I asked how much time the portal was taking. About an hour every evening.
She decided, right there, to stop using that portal and move the same hour to two other things: messaging alumni from her course for referrals, and registering on our list for visiting companies. Before she left, I introduced her by phone to Vidya, an alumna in audit.
Next step: I'll check in with Rajni in two weeks to see which of the two new channels is getting replies.

qa.q: How many applications had Rajni sent on the portal?
What does I keep thinking the next one will work suggest about Rajni?
qa.a: It suggests Rajni felt stuck and still hopeful, reluctant to give up on an hour a day already invested.

qa.q: What else could Rajni measure going forward?
qa.a: Rajni could keep a small log of messages and replies for each new channel, so the next decision rests on results too.

qa.q: How might Vidya see being contacted about Rajni?
qa.a: Vidya, as an alumna, may be glad to help someone from her own course and can offer a direct route a portal never gave.

grounding: Shows a student dropping a portal after thirty unanswered applications and moving the same time to alumni referrals and the placement cell.

subtype: Approach: cutting losses on a low-yield channel [Revision]
passage:
Thursday
Thirty. I counted today. Thirty applications on that one job site since August, and not one reply. Not even a rejection mail.
I kept telling myself it needs time. But Trisha got two interviews in the same month through the college placement cell and a referral from her cousin's senior. She didn't send thirty of anything.
So tonight I did the painful thing. Deleted the app from my phone. Wrote down how long it was eating: roughly an hour every night.
New plan for that same hour:
Mon/Wed/Fri: message two alumni from our department
Tue/Thu: update my file with the placement cell and check their company list
Trisha's coming with me to the placement office tomorrow at 11.
It feels like quitting. It isn't. It's moving the hour to where doors actually open.
Indu

qa.q: When is Indu going to the placement office?
Why does deleting the app feel hard for Indu?
qa.a: Indu feels reluctant and sad, as if quitting, since it is painful to give up on so much time already spent, even without a single reply.

qa.q: What else could Indu do to judge the new plan?
qa.a: Indu could count messages and replies for a few weeks, so Indu can see which channel works and adjust again.

qa.q: How might Trisha see Indu's decision?
qa.a: Trisha, whose interviews came through the placement cell and a referral, would likely support it, and is going along to the office.

grounding: Illustrates a student cutting losses on a job site after thirty silent applications and moving that hour to alumni and the placement cell.
